headline: Councillors heard police and outreach updates on Salem's camping ordinance; voted 4-1 to keep the matter in committee.
summary: The meeting covered police and outreach reports on encampments, arrests, shelter availability, and storage under the camping ordinance. No changes to the ordinance were voted on. Another meeting on possible ordinance changes is planned for mid-October.

decision_evidence.quote: Councillor Smith motions to remain in committee and seconded by Councillor Holappa. Motion carries 4-1.

plain_text:
City of Salem, Massachusetts 
 
“Know Your Rights Under the Open Meeting Law, M.G.L. c. 30A ss. 18-25 and  
City Ordinance Sections 2-2028 through 2-2033.” 
 
The City Council Committee on     Public Health, Safety and Environment co-posted with the Committee of the 
Whole______________________________________________________________________________________  
met in the Council Chamber on _September 23, 2026__________________ at ______6:00_______P.M. 
for the purpose of discussing the matters(s) listed below.  Notice of this meeting was posted on  
___ July 15, 2026_ at ___        4:39 PM__________________________________________________________ 
(This meeting is being recorded) 
ATTENDANCE 
PHSE – Hapworth (chair), Holappa, Smith, Flynn and Davis.  COW – Merkl, King, Turowski, Sydoriak and Varela. Also attending: 
From police department – Chief Miller, Captain Burke, Seargent Pellitier.  From LifeBridge – Mike King.  From Essex County 
Outreach – Steve Perry. From the city – Solicitor James Wellock. 
ABSENT WERE:  COW – Prosniewski. 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 
#134 The Camping Ordinance to review the policy and get updates from our Police Department 
Hapworth - Before we begin, I want to be clear about the purpose and scope of tonight’s meeting. This meeting was ordered 
by Councillor Davis to discuss the implementation of Salem’s camping ordinance and to hear directly from our public safety 
officials and nonprofit providers about how the ordinance has been working in practice. That is the matter that came before 
the committee, and that is how tonight’s meeting was publicly posted. 
Under the Open Meeting Law, meeting notices are required to identify with reasonable specificity the matters the chair 
anticipates will be discussed. The Attorney General has further advised that when a controversial or high-interest matter is not 
included on a meeting notice, discussion or action on that matter should generally be postponed until it is properly noticed. 
The City Solicitor has advised this committee that motions tonight to amend, substantially change, or repeal the camping 
ordinance could exceed the scope of the posted meeting and create an Open Meeting Law issue. Every councillor is 
responsible for exercising their own judgment. I am not going to prevent a member from making an otherwise procedurally 
proper motion solely because counsel has advised against it. 
However, I want the legal advice stated clearly and placed on the record before we begin. If a member chooses to proceed 
contrary to that advice, they should do so understanding that the Attorney General can determine whether individual 
members were responsible for an Open Meeting Law violation and whether any violation was intentional and contrary to legal 
advice. 
My intention as chair tonight is therefore to keep the discussion focused on the matter that was actually posted: how the 
ordinance has been implemented, what our public safety officials and service providers have experienced, what has worked, 
what has not, and what we can learn from their experience.
Additionally, for the attendees, I just want to ask that we please respect the rules of decorum and that we all abide by the rules 
in these chambers. That means no interruptions, side conversations, calling out, clapping, cheering, booing, or jeering during 
the meeting. 
Under Massachusetts General Law, attendees must remain silent when requested by the chair and may not disrupt 
proceedings. These rules will apply equally to everyone. I ask that we respect the chamber and allow the meeting to proceed in 
an orderly way. 
Presentation Summary 
Captain John Burke of the Salem Police Department presented an update on the city’s camping ordinance and the Police 
Department’s experience with homeless encampments. He explained that he supervises the Community Impact Unit (CIU), 
which works with unhoused individuals as well as people experiencing mental health and substance-use issues. He also 
recognized the CIU team, including Seargent Pellitier, Officer Ted Pierce, Officer Neil Sicard, Mental Health Clinician, Jocelyn 
White, and the Essex County Outreach Worker, Steve Perry, for their role in responding to encampments and connecting 
people with services.  
Captain Burke began by reviewing the history of encampments in Salem, starting with Old Town Hall in 2023 and later 
expanding to substantial encampments along the South River near Congress and Lafayette Streets, including areas near 
Wendy’s and National Grid property. He described the encampments as involving tents, abandoned belongings, furniture, 
trash, pallets, and other debris. During this period, police recorded 241 calls for service, 35 arrests, 68 medical assists, 12 
overdoses, reports of assaults and other disturbances, and 49 reports from Wendy’s involving trespassing and unwanted 
parties.  
The presentation also focused on health and safety conditions at the encampments. Burke described discarded hypodermic 
needles, rats, trash, open fires, and other hazards. He reported that Department of Public Services employees had experienced 
two confirmed needle-stick injuries and two additional reported incidents over the previous three years. He also showed 
images and videos illustrating fights, drug-related concerns, rodents, and unsafe conditions. Other encampment locations, 
including Castle Hill Park, the area near the train tracks on Grove Street, and an area behind 400 Highland Avenue, were 
described as having significant debris, fires, or other safety concerns.  
Burke then discussed the implementation of the camping ordinance. Since its passage in June 2024, the CIU had advised 
people to vacate encampments approximately 92 times. He said the department had made only three arrests involving two 
individuals and emphasized that arrests were not the department’s goal. Officers frequently provided additional time when 
people were taking steps to comply, sometimes returning 13 to 24 hours later without making an arrest. He also said that 
virtually no one had requested that the Police Department store their belongings, with one exception that he characterized as 
unrelated to the intended purpose of the ordinance.  
Burke credited outreach workers and mental health and social-service providers with helping people transition from 
encampments. He said that when the South River encampment was closed, approximately 10 former residents were helped 
into better circumstances, including more stable housing and family reunification. He stated that the closure itself helped make 
some individuals more receptive to outreach services. He also cited increased numbers of unhoused individuals living on the 
streets, stating that approximately 95 people had been identified as currently living on the streets in Salem, compared with 
roughly 15 people who had consistently been living on the streets in prior years.  
The presentation concluded with current concerns about people congregating at Riley Plaza and Charlotte Forten Park. Burke 
described reports involving drinking, public defecation, drug use, and fighting, and said lighting had been installed at Charlotte 
Forten Park because of safety concerns. He cited two recent violent incidents there, including an assault involving a skateboard 
and an incident in which officers responded to a reported knife assault and became involved in a physical struggle with an 
individual. He also presented police incident numbers involving unhoused individuals, which he said had increased in recent 
years. Burke concluded that, in his experience, concentrated encampments had consistently been associated with violence, 
substance abuse, health hazards, and fire risks, while acknowledging that not every individual tent or dispersed location 
presented the same problems. He emphasized the impact encampments had on public spaces and neighborhood residents and 
invited outreach worker Steve Perry to speak about his work.
Steve Perry of Essex County Outreach described his work with the CIU during the South River encampment, emphasizing a 
humane, individualized approach to connecting people with services. Drawing on his own recovery experience, he said 
outreach workers went tent-to-tent to learn about each person’s circumstances, including mental health and substance use 
issues, family connections, and immediate needs. Rather than forcing people out, the team spent six to eight months building 
trust, providing basic necessities, and giving individuals time to consider options such as detox, intensive outpatient treatment, 
or other programs. 
Perry said the outreach effort successfully connected people with treatment, temporary housing, apartments, and family 
members, working with police and organizations such as LifeBridge to provide support. He argued that simply leaving people in 
the encampment would perpetuate substance use and potentially lead to more overdoses and violence. Based on his 
experience, he expressed support for a treatment-focused approach and said his organization was willing to continue helping 
people access appropriate services. 
Councillor King asked about the circumstances surrounding the 92 instances in which individuals were advised to vacate 
encampments, including what typically prompted the interaction and how the notices were delivered. She was told that when 
overflow shelter was available, officers would respond quickly to new encampments, explain available options such as 
overflow shelter or LifeBridge, and provide a notice allowing 12 hours to leave, with additional time when needed. Captain 
Burke said most interactions were cooperative. King also asked whether the city sought shelter options outside Salem. She was 
told that LifeBridge and the local overflow shelter were generally the only available options, and that other shelters or police 
departments sometimes directed people toward Salem instead. 
King also questioned the three arrests associated with the ordinance, including concerns about criminalizing homelessness. 
She was told that in one case, an individual repeatedly refused available accommodations even after arrangements had been 
made for belongings and pets, while the other case involved multiple warnings before the arrest. Officials emphasized that 
arrests were made only after repeated warnings and that violations of city ordinances do not result in a Massachusetts criminal 
record or prolonged incarceration; those arrested were released the same day or the following day. 
Councillor Holappa questioned Captain Burke about trends in homelessness and enforcement under the camping ordinance. 
She estimated that approximately 30 people were living in encampments in 2024, compared with about 95 currently, and 
asked whether enforcement incidents had also increased. The captain confirmed that the earlier encampment figures were 
rough estimates and represented the largest concentrations, with numbers fluctuating over time, and agreed that the number 
of unhoused people had increased substantially and that incidents appeared to be rising slightly. Holappa then asked what 
typically triggered the 92 written warnings and whether they were primarily based on complaints or the availability of shelter. 
The captain explained that when shelter was available—particularly when the overflow shelter was operating, or when 
LifeBridge could provide a specific placement—that was generally the basis for enforcement. Although health or safety hazards 
could also provide grounds for action, officers generally relied on shelter availability rather than those conditions. 
Holappa further clarified if the shelter was considered unavailable when facilities were full, unless officers could secure an 
individual placement. The captain confirmed that most of the 92 enforcement instances occurred when a bed could be 
secured, although a small number may have involved health hazards or other circumstances. Holappa then read the stated 
purpose of the camping ordinance, which includes promoting public health and safety, providing available shelter and housing, 
ensuring reasonable access to services, and connecting people with supportive resources. She asked whether, based on the 
discussion, the captain believed the ordinance had fulfilled its purpose. The captain responded that the ordinance had 
absolutely helped. Holappa then summarized the figures, noting that the number of people experiencing homelessness had at 
least doubled while incidents remained roughly similar and 92 people had been moved into shelter during the period, setting 
up a question about the relationship between the ordinance’s stated goals and its outcomes. 
Councillor Merkl thanked the Captain and CIU for their work assisting people experiencing homelessness, including 
partnerships with Essex County Outreach and LifeBridge. She appreciated the team’s approach of trying to avoid arrests and 
giving individuals time to comply. Merkl then raised concerns about unattended belongings in public areas, particularly near 
the train station, noting that residents may be uneasy when packages, backpacks, or other items are left unattended for 
extended periods. She asked what procedures and timelines the police use to determine whether such property is abandoned, 
hazardous, or belongs to someone experiencing homelessness. Merkl also asked whether current encampments present 
environmental and safety concerns similar to those seen during the extensive South River cleanup in 2024, which involved 
contamination and the temporary closure of a park.
In response, the captain said the contamination seen at South River was unusually extensive, but that smaller-scale sanitation 
and environmental problems remain common at encampments. They noted that trash can accumulate where there are no 
waste facilities and that outdoor areas are sometimes used as restrooms, although some individuals make efforts to keep their 
areas clean. Regarding unattended property, Chief Miller explained that police must make a case-by-case judgment about 
whether an item is ordinary discarded material, a health hazard, potentially dangerous, or someone's personal belongings. 
Clearly discarded or deteriorated items can be removed by DPW, while suspicious items may require the police explosives-
detection dog to ensure safety. Property known to belong to an unhoused person presents a more difficult situation, 
particularly when officers know the person is temporarily away and intends to return. Captain Burke said the CIU’s knowledge 
of individuals and their belongings help officers distinguish between abandoned property and possessions that someone is 
likely to reclaim. 
Councillor Flynn thanked the captain, police officers, social workers, and outreach workers for their work, emphasizing that 
they see the conditions firsthand and that he believes their efforts have made conditions safer for both unhoused individuals 
and residents. He asked whether the current camping ordinance was working and whether the captain recommended any 
changes. The captain said the ordinance had been very helpful and was serving its purpose. He said he would prefer having 
somewhat greater discretion to determine whether particular locations or circumstances were safe or appropriate, particularly 
when shelter is available, but acknowledged that the Council would decide the ordinance’s final provisions. Regarding the 
property provisions, he said the department had anticipated needing storage space and even purchased a storage container, 
but the provision had not been used; he said he needed to give further thought to what changes might improve the ordinance. 
Flynn also described his firsthand experience with encampments in Ward 4, particularly in wooded areas near Gallows Hill Park 
between 2018 and 2021. He said he had personally observed needles, human waste, trash, people moving through nearby 
yards, a stolen vehicle, and an overdose, and said encampments tended to return after being cleared. He also referenced a 
more recent double homicide behind Walmart and expressed concern about the safety of both unhoused people and nearby 
residents. As a former firefighter, Flynn additionally raised concerns about fires in wooded areas during dry periods and their 
proximity to nearby condominiums. He said his priority was the safety of both housed and unhoused residents, expressed trust 
in the police and outreach professionals, and concluded that based on their assessment that the ordinance was working, he 
supported keeping it in its current form. 
Councillor Davis questioned the captain about the 92 individuals who were moved, seeking clarification on how many were 
moved when shelter was not available and what circumstances justified those actions. The captain said the department could 
not readily provide an exact number because officers had to review hundreds of reports but indicated that most moves 
occurred when shelter was available. Davis also asked for a clearer definition of “unsafe conditions,” noting that simply 
camping could broadly be characterized as unsafe or unhealthy. The captain said he would consider factors such as fires, 
significant violence or assaults, large numbers of hypodermic needles, and proximity to sensitive locations such as schools, 
while ordinary trash alone would generally not meet the threshold. 
Davis also questioned the notice given to people being ordered to leave, noting that the written form does not identify the 
specific reason for the action. He expressed concern that this could create confusion about what is and is not prohibited under 
the ordinance and suggested more specific notices and proactive communication with unhoused people. The captain said 
officers generally explain the reason in person and often have ongoing conversations with people, although he acknowledged 
that communication could always be improved. Davis also asked about reports of police slashing tents.  Captain Burke said this 
was not current police procedure and had not been done by the current captain, although it may have occurred decades ago. 
Finally, Davis raised concerns that arrests under the ordinance could potentially affect housing or employment even if they do 
not appear on a Massachusetts CORI record. Captain Burke explained that ordinance violations do not appear on CORI, 
although arrest records are public and could potentially be obtained through a public-records request. He clarified that one 
person arrested twice had previously been offered two years of housing but declined to comply with its rules, while another 
arrest involved an assault-and-battery charge after the person threw a water bottle at a bicyclist; the arrest would have 
occurred regardless of the camping charge. Davis also asked whether officers consider legitimate reasons for declining shelter, 
such as restrictions involving pets, family, employment, or personal safety. The captain said they would consider specific 
circumstances, particularly if a person faced a known risk of victimization at the proposed shelter and could honor such a 
concern when warranted.
Councillor Turowski thanked Captain Burke, Chief Miller, and the Police Department for their transparency and ongoing 
attention to the issue, noting that she has attended numerous Point and Downtown neighborhood meetings where police 
have consistently answered residents’ questions. She described her own experience walking along the south side of the harbor 
after COVID and eventually stopping because she no longer felt safe, viewing that as a loss of public space. Turowski echoed 
concerns about unattended belongings in Charlotte Forten Park, particularly from a public-safety and security perspective, 
given residents’ concerns about objects being left under tarps or in piles for days. She acknowledged that the items are 
people’s property but questioned how police can determine whether unattended belongings present a security risk. 
Turowski also asked whether Salem’s increase in people experiencing homelessness—from roughly 65–70 people previously 
identified as housing insecure to about 95 people currently living outside—was consistent with national trends. Captain Burke 
responded that homelessness is increasing nationally but that some communities are bearing a disproportionate share of the 
burden. He said Salem appears to be serving a substantial portion of the North Shore, noting that people have come to Salem 
from other communities because its services and shelter resources are available. He suggested that a more regional approach, 
in which communities provide emergency shelter capacity based on population or need, could distribute responsibility more 
evenly. 
Turowski then asked what prompted the recent installation of lights at Charlotte Forten Park. Captain Burke said the decision 
was based primarily on concerns raised by officers about certain individuals who had taken up residence in the area and his 
review of their histories, rather than a single resident complaint or incident. Finally, Turowski asked about the nature of 
physical violence occurring in the park and whether it typically involved unhoused people or passersby. Captain Burke said the 
violence generally involved one unhoused individual having an issue with another unhoused individual, although there have 
been incidents involving others. 
Councillor Sydoriak thanked Captain Burke and the Police Department for their work with CIU, particularly their efforts to 
connect unhoused individuals with mental health services despite limited resources. He asked about police monitoring of 
encampments in wooded areas, including behind the middle school and in Salem Woods, noting that trash and tents remain in 
some locations. Captain Burke said the department has used drones on a limited basis to identify encampments, particularly 
during the period of fires, and conducts directed patrols of wooded areas when circumstances warrant. Police also 
communicate with Department of Public Services personnel about locations requiring attention, although the amount of 
wooded area and difficult terrain makes frequent monitoring of every location difficult. Burke encouraged councilors to report 
areas that may have been overlooked so officers can follow up. 
Sydoriak asked how residents should report an encampment that presents a public-safety concern. Burke said emergencies 
should be reported through 911, while issues requiring immediate police attention should be reported through the 1212 
line so a patrol officer can respond and refer the matter to the CIU. Non-emergency concerns can also be directed to CIU 
officers by email through the department’s website. Sydoriak then asked about reducing the notice period from 24 to 12 
hours. Burke said 12 hours was generally sufficient to allow people to remove an encampment, although officers often 
provided substantially more time and gave additional time in larger situations such as the South River encampment. He said 
the shorter period gave officers more flexibility when shelter was available and a site needed to be closed. 
Finally, Sydoriak asked what constitutes actually moving when someone is directed to leave an encampment, such as moving 
to another part of Salem Woods. Burke said simply moving a short distance would generally not be considered compliance, 
although officers use discretion depending on the circumstances. He said some individuals had attempted to move only slightly 
to avoid enforcement, but officers tried to monitor those situations. When shelter was available and an individual had been 
given a specific place to go but chose to remain outside, Burke considered that a violation, although he emphasized that 
enforcement in those circumstances was relatively limited. 
Councillor King asked about the storage provision in the notice, noting that people are given 12 hours to vacate but the Salem 
Police Station accepts stored belongings only from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Monday through Friday. She questioned whether officers 
take those limited hours into account when issuing notices and whether transportation could be provided if someone wanted 
to use the storage option but could not get their belongings to the station. Captain Burke said the storage option has rarely 
been used because people generally do not want to turn their property over to police. He said that if someone did request 
assistance, the department would work out a reasonable solution, but that situation had not yet occurred.
King also asked whether officers consider the time of day when issuing a 12-hour notice and provide additional time when the 
notice is issued at an inconvenient hour. Burke explained that CIU officers work during the day and evening and that officers 
would not arrive at 4 or 6 a.m. simply because 12 hours had elapsed. King observed that the department’s responses 
suggested officers use considerable discretion and try to enforce the ordinance reasonably. She asked whether Burke believed 
there was misinformation about how the ordinance is actually enforced and whether clearer ordinance language that better 
reflected current enforcement practices might reduce that misinformation. Burke agreed that misinformation probably exists 
and said clearer language possibly could help. 
Councillor Holappa asked Captain Burke to clarify what the department does when shelter is unavailable. Burke said officers 
may still request that someone move if there are concerns with a location, even when they do not have a legal mechanism to 
enforce the request. He distinguished a request from a lawful order by noting that, in the limited cases involving arrests, 
officers explicitly tell individuals they will be arrested if they do not comply. Holappa also asked whether people might 
misunderstand the difference between a voluntary request and a lawful order; Burke acknowledged that they might. 
Holappa then questioned City Solicitor James Wellock about how Salem’s ordinance interacts with federal and Massachusetts 
law. Wellock explained that the U.S. Supreme Court’s Grants Pass decision held that enforcing laws prohibiting camping 
against people experiencing homelessness does not, by itself, constitute cruel and unusual punishment under the federal 
Constitution. He said there was no binding Massachusetts case law he was aware of addressing the same issue under the state 
constitution, although it remained possible that a future court could interpret the state constitution differently. Wellock also 
said the Massachusetts Attorney General’s Office has invalidated some town bylaws on vagueness and constitutional grounds 
and has interpreted the state constitution as prohibiting ordinances that criminalize camping by homeless people. He clarified, 
however, that the Attorney General’s review authority applies to town bylaws and does not extend in the same manner to 
Salem’s municipal ordinances. 
Councillor Smith thanked Captain Burke and the Police Department, emphasizing the department’s extensive knowledge of 
people experiencing homelessness and its work connecting them with shelter, permanent supportive housing, and other 
services. Smith asked about the prevalence of mental health and substance-use issues among unhoused individuals. Burke 
estimated that the vast majority have some degree of mental health issues and roughly 70% appear to have substance-use 
issues, while noting that officers are not diagnosing people. Smith also asked about the additional municipal costs associated 
with responding to homelessness. Burke said these calls can involve police cruisers as well as fire and ambulance resources, 
and the department has an entire unit dedicated to the issue, although he could not provide a per-person cost. 
Smith then asked whether larger encampments attract additional people and whether Salem’s ordinance might be too lenient. 
Burke said he does not support encampments and believes large concentrations create additional problems because people 
with different challenges are concentrated in one location. He said the former South River encampment attracted drug dealers 
because of the concentration of potential customers, as well as others seeking a place where they believed it was easier to 
engage in certain behaviors. Burke also said some unhoused individuals told officers that they came to Salem because they 
believed it was easier to stay there than in other communities. Smith suggested that strengthening the camping ordinance 
could potentially reduce that influx, and Burke said he would support such an approach. Smith also raised the possibility of 
legally limiting the number or size of tents in a particular area. 
Finally, Smith asked Mike King from LifeBridge whether there were plans to reopen the Transition Center or otherwise expand 
shelter capacity. King said there was nothing immediately planned, but the organization remained willing to operate the center 
because it recognized the need. He explained that reopening was dependent on obtaining funding and that the organization 
was prepared to resume operations if funding became available. 
Public Comment  
Residents & business owners expressed a range of concerns about homelessness, encampments, and enforcement of the 
ordinance. Several residents described impacts on neighborhoods and businesses, including fire, cleanup costs, encampments 
on private or conservation land, and concerns about encampments in public spaces such as playgrounds. Others questioned 
whether existing laws and park restrictions were being consistently enforced and called for clearer enforcement standards, 
better communication between police and affected residents, and sufficient evidence to support enforcement decisions. One 
speaker also criticized the one-minute public-comment limit as inadequate for addressing such a complex issue.
Other commenters emphasized that homelessness requires a broader response than enforcement or prohibiting 
encampments. Speakers pointed to rising housing costs, poverty, mental-health and substance-use services, shelter, and 
transitional programs as contributing factors and potential parts of a longer-term solution. Several residents praised the Police 
Department for using compassion and discretion when responding to unhoused individuals, while cautioning that changes to 
the ordinance should not unnecessarily limit that discretion. Others argued that prohibiting encampments without providing 
housing or alternative services could simply cause people to move repeatedly for one encampment to another, and called for 
greater input from service providers, public-health professionals, and people with direct experience of homelessness. 
Hapworth – We will be scheduling another committee meeting in mid-October to discuss changes to the ordinance that we 
may want to consider.  That wasn’t part of the agenda tonight, but it will be in the near future. 
Councillor Smith motions to remain in committee and seconded by Councillor Holappa.  Motion carries 4-1.   
On the motion of C. Smith, the meeting adjourned at 8:11 P.M.
